medical.title: Brain-computer interface study sheds light on 'mirror neurons'
medical.summary: Scientists have known for years that neural activity in the brain's motor cortex doesn't just happen when people perform actions. Neurons associated with actions—reaching with a hand to grasp an object, for example—also fire when a person watches someone else perform an action. This observational activity, which underlies a concept known as "mirror neurons," may play a role in how humans and other primates learn to perform physical tasks.

medical.title: Hearing loss barriers leave many struggling in silence
medical.summary: Hearing loss affects much more than a person's ability to hear, often affecting relationships, social participation, emotional well-being and quality of life—but despite the availability of support, many people are reluctant to ask for help.

medical.title: Gentle rhythmic tapping on shinbone helps injured brains heal faster in animal models
medical.summary: A traumatic brain injury (TBI) can turn a person's life upside down, leaving lasting effects on memory, thinking, physical abilities and overall quality of life. TBI remains one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. Yet, paradoxically, the same injury that harms the brain may sometimes appear to benefit a broken bone by speeding up healing. In a recent study published in Nature Neuroscience, researchers explored whether the reverse is true.

medical.title: Examining racial disparities in patient adherence to diabetes medications
medical.summary: A new study led by UCLA Health found that a large percentage of disadvantaged patients are not taking their diabetes medications consistently. The analysis of national health records for 587,000 Medicare Advantage patients showed Black and Hispanic patients were less likely than white patients to adhere to their medication protocols.

medical.title: Safer alternative for hormone replacement therapy during menopause proposed
medical.summary: When it comes to balancing hormonal changes during the transition to menopause, less can be more. Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil demonstrated this when testing an alternative to conventional therapy. Rather than replacing estrogen, the team activated only one type of estrogen receptor in cells. This approach had broad metabolic benefits without stimulating the growth of reproductive tissues, such as the uterus and breasts. That is important for individuals with a genetic predisposition to developing tumors.

medical.title: Nearly 1 in 5 people with sight loss report encountering bogus treatments
medical.summary: An international study of almost 1,000 people living with sight loss, led by University College London (UCL) researchers, found that nearly one in five reported receiving or encountering eye treatments they believed to be "bogus."

medical.title: Study of families sheds new light on postpartum depression, its duration and potential solutions
medical.summary: Becoming a parent is a major life change. In addition to fatigue and changes in daily routine, daunting questions arise: Am I taking good care of my baby? Am I doing the right things? Am I up to the job? It is common for mothers experiencing postpartum depression to doubt themselves.

medical.title: Fighting depression with humor: Laughter can bring relief, but not every moment is right
medical.summary: Comedian Robin Williams once said that every time you get depressed, comedy will be there to drag you out of it. But does humor really help? A researcher from SWPS University investigated the potential of using humor to treat depressive states. She found that while it could act as a natural stress buffer, it typically does more harm than good during the acute phase of the illness.

medical.title: Smart contact lens detects serotonin changes in tear samples collected during stress test
medical.summary: A research team led by Dr. Yangzhi Zhu, principal investigator and assistant professor at the Terasaki Institute for Biomedical Innovation, has developed a soft, reusable smart contact lens as part of its broader Ocular Library for the Analysis of Tear Biomarkers (OCULAB), a tear bioelectronics platform for noninvasive, longitudinal biochemical monitoring through the ocular surface and tear film. In this study, the platform was used to measure serotonin directly from tears as a proof-of-concept target for monitoring stress-related physiological changes.

medical.title: New diagnostic test for MS is less painful for patients, leads to a quicker diagnosis and cost savings
medical.summary: A new test to diagnose multiple sclerosis (MS) using an MRI scan instead of a painful spinal tap has been successfully introduced at an NHS trust in England. Researchers at the University of Nottingham previously found that a new type of MRI scan could identify MS with only an extra six minutes in the scanner, meaning patients no longer had to undergo a painful lumbar puncture. The test is now in use in Nottingham and increasingly in other neurology departments worldwide.

medical.title: Astrocytes could help track the timing of frightening experiences
medical.summary: When the brain forms memories of past experiences, it typically encodes various information, including what happened, where it happened and the order in which events unfolded. The hippocampus is one of the primary brain regions involved in forming memories.

medical.title: New study reveals differences in gestational diabetes between social groups
medical.summary: Gestational diabetes has become increasingly common in Sweden, particularly among women with less education, lower incomes and those born outside the country, according to a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism. The researchers also found that the relationship between gestational diabetes and complications during pregnancy and childbirth differs among population groups.

medical.title: Synthetic molecule improves mitochondrial function in ALS models and patient-derived stem cells
medical.summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease in which motor neurons are gradually lost, leading to muscle weakness and, as the disease advances, difficulty breathing and swallowing. Existing medicines can slow disease progression to some extent, but no treatment has been established that fundamentally reverses the disease process. Mitochondrial dysfunction is considered a potential therapeutic target because mitochondria play a central role in cellular energy production and are frequently impaired in ALS.

medical.title: Health communication expert finds GLP-1 users face stigma within their social circles
medical.summary: People taking popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound may face stigma from those closest to them, according to a new study by a Florida State University professor.

medical.title: How the APOE4 gene damages brain blood vessels in Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: Mount Sinai researchers have identified how APOE4, the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, damages the brain's blood vessels and promotes the buildup of abnormal proteins linked to neurodegenerative disease. Published in Cell and Cell Stem Cell, the studies identify potentially reversible disease mechanisms and demonstrate how a new stem cell-derived human brain tissue platform can accelerate mechanistic discovery and therapeutic development.

medical.title: Multiple childhood traumas tied to worse young adult outcomes
medical.summary: Emerging adults with an average age of 19 who experienced four or more adverse childhood experiences had substantially higher rates of depression, suicidal ideation, hard drug use and interpersonal violence than those who reported no childhood adversity.

medical.title: Immune cells reveal widespread SMN protein loss in spinal muscular atrophy
medical.summary: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a neurodegenerative disorder that leads to muscle loss and can severely impair the mobility of those affected. It is usually caused by a defect in the SMN1 gene, which is expressed in all cells of the body. Whether this mutation also affects the immune system remains largely underexplored. That is precisely what researchers from TWINCORE, the Center for Experimental and Clinical Infection Research, and Hannover Medical School (MHH) have now investigated. Their findings have been published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

medical.title: Data expertise helps researchers understand clinical tools usage
medical.summary: Clinical decision-support tools have the potential to help clinicians make evidence-based decisions, access relevant patient information and navigate complex care. However, making a tool available in an electronic health record (EHR) does not guarantee that clinicians will use it in routine practice.

medical.title: Is mindfulness linked to better mental health and lower self-stigma among university students?
medical.summary: Being made to feel different, lesser or unwanted can be a common experience for many minority groups. When people are excluded or denied full social acceptance because they are perceived as having a "lesser" status or value, they may internalize that stigma.

medical.title: Breath tests could distinguish cancerous lung nodules from benign ones
medical.summary: Human breath could help identify cancerous lung nodules and reduce the need for invasive testing. New Griffith University research analyzed exhaled breath to help doctors distinguish between cancerous and noncancerous lung nodules, supporting earlier lung cancer diagnosis. Approximately 2.5 million new cases of lung cancer are diagnosed each year.

medical.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
medical.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

medical.title: AI tool finds biological signals in the gut microbiome that other methods miss, may flag early signs of disease
medical.summary: University of Missouri researchers are using artificial intelligence to uncover hidden clues among the trillions of bacteria living in the human gut, including changes that could one day help scientists detect diseases earlier. The Mizzou team—which brings together expertise in medicine, data science and engineering—developed a new machine-learning tool capable of finding biological signals that conventional methods miss. Their paper is published in the journal mSystems.

medical.title: Chronic stress linked to differences in cognitive decline across certain demographic groups, study finds
medical.summary: Chronic stress and perceived social support may play a role in how memory and thinking abilities change with age, according to a new study led by researchers at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.

medical.title: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
medical.summary: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.

medical.title: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
medical.summary: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

science.title: New AlphaFold Database release adds viral protein complexes to support pandemic preparedness
science.summary: AI-predicted protein complex structures for more than 2,800 viruses are now openly available in the AlphaFold Database. To better understand and protect against emerging pathogens, the dataset prioritizes proteomes from viral families known to infect humans.

science.title: Sharks can hear sounds nearly 250 feet away and find the source
science.summary: Sound travels through the ocean carrying clues about potential prey, predators and other animals, giving sharks an important way to detect what they cannot yet see. But exactly how far a free-swimming shark can hear a sound—and whether it can determine where that sound is coming from—has remained largely unknown.

science.title: Is the universe twisted? A new check on a possible twist in the universe's oldest light
science.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the universe's oldest light, leftover thermal radiation from about 380,000 years after the big bang. Maps of the CMB offer a picture of the "baby universe" as it was 13.8 billion years ago.

science.title: Greenland ice shelf weakened by estuary ahead of recent calving event
science.summary: In August 2026, an iceberg the size of Manhattan broke away from the Petermann Ice Shelf in northern Greenland. It was the glacier's largest calving event since 2020. Long before the breakup, CIRES scientists were developing a new method to understand the planet's first known ice shelf estuary on the Petermann Ice Shelf.

science.title: Montreal's squirrels provide insight into evolutionary change in urban species
science.summary: By comparing variations in the coat colors of eastern gray squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) in Montreal city parks, researchers found that hyperlocal conditions appear to play a bigger role in shaping wildlife traits than previously thought.

science.title: Hurricane Polo triggers huge waves in coastal Mexican city
science.summary: Hurricane Polo swirled menacingly along Mexico's southern coast Thursday, triggering towering waves in a Pacific port city.

science.title: NASA’s Machines for Mars Make Beer Bubbly
science.summary: Carbon-capture technology repurposed for breweries spreads and finds new applications

science.title: Family resilience can help protect children from climate change
science.summary: As climate change brings more extreme weather events, strengthening families before disasters strike can help protect children's health and well-being, says Mary McKay, a professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on child mental health.

science.title: Mistletoe berry glue bonds even nonstick Teflon and can be reactivated with heat
science.summary: Mistletoe is best known from winter traditions as a symbol of luck and affection. For trees, however, the hemiparasitic plant can be a burden: It draws water and nutrients from its hosts. Now the plant could provide a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based industrial adhesives.

science.title: Supernova or black hole: Neutrino 'flavor' may determine the fate of dying stars
science.summary: As a star nears the end of its life, it faces two very different fates: It can explode as a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star, or collapse and become a black hole. What determines the outcome remains one of astrophysics' great unanswered questions.

science.title: Major survey reveals public support for UK nature recovery
science.summary: A new survey from the University of Exeter and the University of Surrey reveals broad public support for policies to protect and restore nature in the U.K. Researchers surveyed almost 3,000 people across the country, exploring their feelings, concerns, opinions and experiences in nature.

science.title: Earth's deep secret: Why your day isn't quite 24 hours
science.summary: You might think the length of a day never varies—exactly 24 hours. You'd be wrong, at least if you count days in milliseconds, as physicists do.

science.title: 'Jumping genes' helped ants in their evolutionary triumph after the extinction of the dinosaurs
science.summary: About 66 million years ago, the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs paved the way for a spectacular expansion of new animal species. During this period, ants rose to ecological dominance. Today, they form the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species worldwide.

science.title: Research grant reviews vary by gender and academic discipline, study finds
science.summary: An analysis of almost 40,000 research funding review reports found that female researchers wrote longer, more positive assessments than their male counterparts and addressed the formal evaluation criteria more comprehensively.

science.title: Astronomers capture an unprecedented view of gas giant formation in action
science.summary: In recent decades, astronomers have reconstructed a fairly complete scenario for planet formation, from minute dust motes clumping together to the emergence of rocky spheres thousands of kilometers across, like Earth, or larger gas giants like Jupiter.

science.title: AI can help correct medical misinformation—when it uses the right tone
science.summary: At a time of rampant medical misinformation online, artificial intelligence can do a good job of correcting falsehoods, but the tone of the correction is key, according to new research led by Washington State University.

science.title: Two-daughter households report greater happiness than son-only households in China
science.summary: In many parts of the world, the birth of a boy is celebrated as a blessing, while the birth of a girl is still viewed as a burden. The disturbing prevalence of female feticide bears witness to this inequality. In countries like China and India, deeply rooted cultural beliefs often place greater value on sons because they are expected to support their parents in old age and carry on the family name. Yet when scientists looked at the numbers, they found that what tradition says should bring parents happiness does not necessarily match what actually does.

science.title: Alaska's orange rivers are more metallic than acid mine drainage
science.summary: The bright orange plumes of water scientists first noticed billowing across a river in Alaska's Brooks Range in 2018 were even more acidic and metallic than water leached from metal mines, despite their pristine surroundings. That's according to a new University of California, Davis, study of six affected watersheds.

science.title: Bronze Age migration in Greece largely involved young adults, skeletal samples suggest
science.summary: Young adults, not families, drove migration in Bronze Age communities. Using skeletal samples from archaeological sites in Greece, researchers mapped mobility during the region's Middle and Late Bronze Age. The study suggests that young people sought out new communities.

science.title: Study challenges assumption that women have more emotional intelligence than men
science.summary: A widely held belief that women have more emotional intelligence than men does not hold up under scrutiny, according to a large study of research spanning three decades.

science.title: Solar farms could do more than generate clean energy—they could also cut dust pollution
science.summary: Solar farms built around China's Gobi Desert could have the unexpected benefit of reducing the dust pollution reaching cities across northern China.

science.title: New resource supports parents of preschoolers with suspected developmental delays
science.summary: McGill researchers have created and validated a virtual coaching program that helps parents of preschoolers with developmental delays navigate assessments, appointments and decisions.

science.title: What rises from the ash? How an island changed in the aftermath of the Anak Krakatau eruption
science.summary: The eruption of the Anak Krakatau volcano in early September 2026 had effects far beyond the rumbling ground and ash that blanketed nearby areas.

science.title: Whirlpool in a water tank reveals long-predicted wave turbulence
science.summary: When water drains from a bathtub, a whirlpool often forms above the drain, and its narrow core can start to wobble and twist. For almost 150 years, physicists have predicted that these wobbles can become turbulent, passing energy from large ripples down to ever smaller ones. Until now, however, this "Kelvin-wave turbulence" had never been seen directly in an experiment.

science.title: 'They wouldn't say it in person': Young gamers reveal their personal experiences in online multiplayer gaming
science.summary: A new UEL research project is exploring practical ways to reduce antisocial and harmful behavior in online gaming while helping platforms create more positive and inclusive experiences for young players.

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Sharks can hear sounds nearly 250 feet away and find the source
mix_items.summary: Sound travels through the ocean carrying clues about potential prey, predators and other animals, giving sharks an important way to detect what they cannot yet see. But exactly how far a free-swimming shark can hear a sound—and whether it can determine where that sound is coming from—has remained largely unknown.

mix_items.summary: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the universe's oldest light, leftover thermal radiation from about 380,000 years after the big bang. Maps of the CMB offer a picture of the "baby universe" as it was 13.8 billion years ago.

mix_items.title: Brain-computer interface study sheds light on 'mirror neurons'
mix_items.summary: Scientists have known for years that neural activity in the brain's motor cortex doesn't just happen when people perform actions. Neurons associated with actions—reaching with a hand to grasp an object, for example—also fire when a person watches someone else perform an action. This observational activity, which underlies a concept known as "mirror neurons," may play a role in how humans and other primates learn to perform physical tasks.

mix_items.title: Greenland ice shelf weakened by estuary ahead of recent calving event
mix_items.summary: In August 2026, an iceberg the size of Manhattan broke away from the Petermann Ice Shelf in northern Greenland. It was the glacier's largest calving event since 2020. Long before the breakup, CIRES scientists were developing a new method to understand the planet's first known ice shelf estuary on the Petermann Ice Shelf.

mix_items.title: Hearing loss barriers leave many struggling in silence
mix_items.summary: Hearing loss affects much more than a person's ability to hear, often affecting relationships, social participation, emotional well-being and quality of life—but despite the availability of support, many people are reluctant to ask for help.

mix_items.title: Gentle rhythmic tapping on shinbone helps injured brains heal faster in animal models
mix_items.summary: A traumatic brain injury (TBI) can turn a person's life upside down, leaving lasting effects on memory, thinking, physical abilities and overall quality of life. TBI remains one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide. Yet, paradoxically, the same injury that harms the brain may sometimes appear to benefit a broken bone by speeding up healing. In a recent study published in Nature Neuroscience, researchers explored whether the reverse is true.

mix_items.title: Examining racial disparities in patient adherence to diabetes medications
mix_items.summary: A new study led by UCLA Health found that a large percentage of disadvantaged patients are not taking their diabetes medications consistently. The analysis of national health records for 587,000 Medicare Advantage patients showed Black and Hispanic patients were less likely than white patients to adhere to their medication protocols.

mix_items.title: Montreal's squirrels provide insight into evolutionary change in urban species
mix_items.summary: By comparing variations in the coat colors of eastern gray squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) in Montreal city parks, researchers found that hyperlocal conditions appear to play a bigger role in shaping wildlife traits than previously thought.

mix_items.summary: Hurricane Polo swirled menacingly along Mexico's southern coast Thursday, triggering towering waves in a Pacific port city.

mix_items.title: Family resilience can help protect children from climate change
mix_items.summary: As climate change brings more extreme weather events, strengthening families before disasters strike can help protect children's health and well-being, says Mary McKay, a professor at the Brown School at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on child mental health.

mix_items.title: Safer alternative for hormone replacement therapy during menopause proposed
mix_items.summary: When it comes to balancing hormonal changes during the transition to menopause, less can be more. Researchers at the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil demonstrated this when testing an alternative to conventional therapy. Rather than replacing estrogen, the team activated only one type of estrogen receptor in cells. This approach had broad metabolic benefits without stimulating the growth of reproductive tissues, such as the uterus and breasts. That is important for individuals with a genetic predisposition to developing tumors.

mix_items.title: Mistletoe berry glue bonds even nonstick Teflon and can be reactivated with heat
mix_items.summary: Mistletoe is best known from winter traditions as a symbol of luck and affection. For trees, however, the hemiparasitic plant can be a burden: It draws water and nutrients from its hosts. Now the plant could provide a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based industrial adhesives.

mix_items.title: Nearly 1 in 5 people with sight loss report encountering bogus treatments
mix_items.summary: An international study of almost 1,000 people living with sight loss, led by University College London (UCL) researchers, found that nearly one in five reported receiving or encountering eye treatments they believed to be "bogus."

mix_items.title: Supernova or black hole: Neutrino 'flavor' may determine the fate of dying stars
mix_items.summary: As a star nears the end of its life, it faces two very different fates: It can explode as a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star, or collapse and become a black hole. What determines the outcome remains one of astrophysics' great unanswered questions.

mix_items.title: Major survey reveals public support for UK nature recovery
mix_items.summary: A new survey from the University of Exeter and the University of Surrey reveals broad public support for policies to protect and restore nature in the U.K. Researchers surveyed almost 3,000 people across the country, exploring their feelings, concerns, opinions and experiences in nature.

mix_items.title: Study of families sheds new light on postpartum depression, its duration and potential solutions
mix_items.summary: Becoming a parent is a major life change. In addition to fatigue and changes in daily routine, daunting questions arise: Am I taking good care of my baby? Am I doing the right things? Am I up to the job? It is common for mothers experiencing postpartum depression to doubt themselves.

mix_items.title: Earth's deep secret: Why your day isn't quite 24 hours
mix_items.summary: You might think the length of a day never varies—exactly 24 hours. You'd be wrong, at least if you count days in milliseconds, as physicists do.

mix_items.title: Fighting depression with humor: Laughter can bring relief, but not every moment is right
mix_items.summary: Comedian Robin Williams once said that every time you get depressed, comedy will be there to drag you out of it. But does humor really help? A researcher from SWPS University investigated the potential of using humor to treat depressive states. She found that while it could act as a natural stress buffer, it typically does more harm than good during the acute phase of the illness.

mix_items.title: Smart contact lens detects serotonin changes in tear samples collected during stress test
mix_items.summary: A research team led by Dr. Yangzhi Zhu, principal investigator and assistant professor at the Terasaki Institute for Biomedical Innovation, has developed a soft, reusable smart contact lens as part of its broader Ocular Library for the Analysis of Tear Biomarkers (OCULAB), a tear bioelectronics platform for noninvasive, longitudinal biochemical monitoring through the ocular surface and tear film. In this study, the platform was used to measure serotonin directly from tears as a proof-of-concept target for monitoring stress-related physiological changes.

mix_items.title: 'Jumping genes' helped ants in their evolutionary triumph after the extinction of the dinosaurs
mix_items.summary: About 66 million years ago, the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs paved the way for a spectacular expansion of new animal species. During this period, ants rose to ecological dominance. Today, they form the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species worldwide.

mix_items.title: Research grant reviews vary by gender and academic discipline, study finds
mix_items.summary: An analysis of almost 40,000 research funding review reports found that female researchers wrote longer, more positive assessments than their male counterparts and addressed the formal evaluation criteria more comprehensively.

mix_items.title: New diagnostic test for MS is less painful for patients, leads to a quicker diagnosis and cost savings
mix_items.summary: A new test to diagnose multiple sclerosis (MS) using an MRI scan instead of a painful spinal tap has been successfully introduced at an NHS trust in England. Researchers at the University of Nottingham previously found that a new type of MRI scan could identify MS with only an extra six minutes in the scanner, meaning patients no longer had to undergo a painful lumbar puncture. The test is now in use in Nottingham and increasingly in other neurology departments worldwide.

mix_items.title: Astrocytes could help track the timing of frightening experiences
mix_items.summary: When the brain forms memories of past experiences, it typically encodes various information, including what happened, where it happened and the order in which events unfolded. The hippocampus is one of the primary brain regions involved in forming memories.

mix_items.title: New study reveals differences in gestational diabetes between social groups
mix_items.summary: Gestational diabetes has become increasingly common in Sweden, particularly among women with less education, lower incomes and those born outside the country, according to a new study from Karolinska Institutet published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism. The researchers also found that the relationship between gestational diabetes and complications during pregnancy and childbirth differs among population groups.

mix_items.title: Astronomers capture an unprecedented view of gas giant formation in action
mix_items.summary: In recent decades, astronomers have reconstructed a fairly complete scenario for planet formation, from minute dust motes clumping together to the emergence of rocky spheres thousands of kilometers across, like Earth, or larger gas giants like Jupiter.

mix_items.title: Synthetic molecule improves mitochondrial function in ALS models and patient-derived stem cells
mix_items.summary: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease in which motor neurons are gradually lost, leading to muscle weakness and, as the disease advances, difficulty breathing and swallowing. Existing medicines can slow disease progression to some extent, but no treatment has been established that fundamentally reverses the disease process. Mitochondrial dysfunction is considered a potential therapeutic target because mitochondria play a central role in cellular energy production and are frequently impaired in ALS.

mix_items.title: AI can help correct medical misinformation—when it uses the right tone
mix_items.summary: At a time of rampant medical misinformation online, artificial intelligence can do a good job of correcting falsehoods, but the tone of the correction is key, according to new research led by Washington State University.

mix_items.title: Two-daughter households report greater happiness than son-only households in China
mix_items.summary: In many parts of the world, the birth of a boy is celebrated as a blessing, while the birth of a girl is still viewed as a burden. The disturbing prevalence of female feticide bears witness to this inequality. In countries like China and India, deeply rooted cultural beliefs often place greater value on sons because they are expected to support their parents in old age and carry on the family name. Yet when scientists looked at the numbers, they found that what tradition says should bring parents happiness does not necessarily match what actually does.

mix_items.title: Alaska's orange rivers are more metallic than acid mine drainage
mix_items.summary: The bright orange plumes of water scientists first noticed billowing across a river in Alaska's Brooks Range in 2018 were even more acidic and metallic than water leached from metal mines, despite their pristine surroundings. That's according to a new University of California, Davis, study of six affected watersheds.

mix_items.title: Bronze Age migration in Greece largely involved young adults, skeletal samples suggest
mix_items.summary: Young adults, not families, drove migration in Bronze Age communities. Using skeletal samples from archaeological sites in Greece, researchers mapped mobility during the region's Middle and Late Bronze Age. The study suggests that young people sought out new communities.

mix_items.title: Health communication expert finds GLP-1 users face stigma within their social circles
mix_items.summary: People taking popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound may face stigma from those closest to them, according to a new study by a Florida State University professor.

mix_items.title: How the APOE4 gene damages brain blood vessels in Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: Mount Sinai researchers have identified how APOE4, the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, damages the brain's blood vessels and promotes the buildup of abnormal proteins linked to neurodegenerative disease. Published in Cell and Cell Stem Cell, the studies identify potentially reversible disease mechanisms and demonstrate how a new stem cell-derived human brain tissue platform can accelerate mechanistic discovery and therapeutic development.

mix_items.title: Multiple childhood traumas tied to worse young adult outcomes
mix_items.summary: Emerging adults with an average age of 19 who experienced four or more adverse childhood experiences had substantially higher rates of depression, suicidal ideation, hard drug use and interpersonal violence than those who reported no childhood adversity.

mix_items.title: Study challenges assumption that women have more emotional intelligence than men
mix_items.summary: A widely held belief that women have more emotional intelligence than men does not hold up under scrutiny, according to a large study of research spanning three decades.

mix_items.title: Solar farms could do more than generate clean energy—they could also cut dust pollution
mix_items.summary: Solar farms built around China's Gobi Desert could have the unexpected benefit of reducing the dust pollution reaching cities across northern China.

mix_items.title: Immune cells reveal widespread SMN protein loss in spinal muscular atrophy
mix_items.summary: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a neurodegenerative disorder that leads to muscle loss and can severely impair the mobility of those affected. It is usually caused by a defect in the SMN1 gene, which is expressed in all cells of the body. Whether this mutation also affects the immune system remains largely underexplored. That is precisely what researchers from TWINCORE, the Center for Experimental and Clinical Infection Research, and Hannover Medical School (MHH) have now investigated. Their findings have been published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.

mix_items.title: New resource supports parents of preschoolers with suspected developmental delays
mix_items.summary: McGill researchers have created and validated a virtual coaching program that helps parents of preschoolers with developmental delays navigate assessments, appointments and decisions.

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: What rises from the ash? How an island changed in the aftermath of the Anak Krakatau eruption
mix_items.summary: The eruption of the Anak Krakatau volcano in early September 2026 had effects far beyond the rumbling ground and ash that blanketed nearby areas.

mix_items.title: Data expertise helps researchers understand clinical tools usage
mix_items.summary: Clinical decision-support tools have the potential to help clinicians make evidence-based decisions, access relevant patient information and navigate complex care. However, making a tool available in an electronic health record (EHR) does not guarantee that clinicians will use it in routine practice.

mix_items.title: Whirlpool in a water tank reveals long-predicted wave turbulence
mix_items.summary: When water drains from a bathtub, a whirlpool often forms above the drain, and its narrow core can start to wobble and twist. For almost 150 years, physicists have predicted that these wobbles can become turbulent, passing energy from large ripples down to ever smaller ones. Until now, however, this "Kelvin-wave turbulence" had never been seen directly in an experiment.

mix_items.title: Is mindfulness linked to better mental health and lower self-stigma among university students?
mix_items.summary: Being made to feel different, lesser or unwanted can be a common experience for many minority groups. When people are excluded or denied full social acceptance because they are perceived as having a "lesser" status or value, they may internalize that stigma.

mix_items.title: 'They wouldn't say it in person': Young gamers reveal their personal experiences in online multiplayer gaming
mix_items.summary: A new UEL research project is exploring practical ways to reduce antisocial and harmful behavior in online gaming while helping platforms create more positive and inclusive experiences for young players.

mix_items.title: Breath tests could distinguish cancerous lung nodules from benign ones
mix_items.summary: Human breath could help identify cancerous lung nodules and reduce the need for invasive testing. New Griffith University research analyzed exhaled breath to help doctors distinguish between cancerous and noncancerous lung nodules, supporting earlier lung cancer diagnosis. Approximately 2.5 million new cases of lung cancer are diagnosed each year.

mix_items.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
mix_items.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: AI tool finds biological signals in the gut microbiome that other methods miss, may flag early signs of disease
mix_items.summary: University of Missouri researchers are using artificial intelligence to uncover hidden clues among the trillions of bacteria living in the human gut, including changes that could one day help scientists detect diseases earlier. The Mizzou team—which brings together expertise in medicine, data science and engineering—developed a new machine-learning tool capable of finding biological signals that conventional methods miss. Their paper is published in the journal mSystems.

mix_items.title: Chronic stress linked to differences in cognitive decline across certain demographic groups, study finds
mix_items.summary: Chronic stress and perceived social support may play a role in how memory and thinking abilities change with age, according to a new study led by researchers at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
mix_items.summary: A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect. The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.

mix_items.title: Aging muscles may be losing strength for a reason scientists missed
mix_items.summary: A newly identified breakdown in communication between nerves and muscles could help explain why people lose strength as they age. Researchers were able to improve muscle strength in an animal model by targeting a key protein, raising hopes that some age-related weakness could eventually be treated.

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
